name: Nyingma (the Ancient / Old Translation school)

tradition.text: founded in the 8th century under King Trisong Detsen, when Padmasambhava, Śāntarakṣita and Vimalamitra taught in Tibet and Samye was built

scholarly.text: the 8th-9th c. imperial translations; the name 'Nyingma' (the old ones) came into use from the 11th c. in contrast to the new (gsar ma) translations

transmissions_received.what: the Indian tantras (Mahāyoga, Anuyoga) and their empowerments, through Padmasambhava, Vimalamitra, Buddhaguhya and the 8th-9th c. translators
Śāntarakṣita's Madhyamaka and the monastic foundation at Samye
the Mūlasarvāstivāda ordination given to the first Tibetan monks (the 'seven men who were tested')

transmissions_given.what: Dzogchen and the Nyingthig combined with Mahāmudrā (the Third Karmapa; Karma Chagme's union of Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen)
the treasure (terma) cycles and Dzogchen that stand at the centre of the non-sectarian movement
shared Dzogchen, treasure and nine-vehicle frameworks (direction disputed; see dsp:bon-and-buddhism)

distinctive_positions: The teaching is ordered as nine vehicles (theg pa rim pa dgu), culminating in the three inner tantras Mahāyoga, Anuyoga and Atiyoga (Dzogchen).
Three streams of transmission: the long lineage of the spoken word (bka' ma), the short lineage of treasures (gter ma) and profound pure visions (dag snang).
The primordial buddha Samantabhadra (Kuntuzangpo) is the dharmakāya teacher; Garab Dorje the first human teacher of Dzogchen; Padmasambhava the 'second Buddha' for Tibet.
The Guhyagarbha is the root Mahāyoga tantra: all phenomena are primordially the maṇḍala of deities — 'great purity and equality' (dag mnyam chen po).

Atiyoga distinguishes awareness (rig pa) from ordinary mind (sems) and teaches the ground as primordial purity and spontaneous presence, realized by cutting through (khregs chod) and direct crossing (thod rgal).
Its tantras (the rnying rgyud) were translated in the first diffusion; their Indian authenticity was disputed by later critics and defended by the school (see dsp:authenticity-of-nyingma-tantras).
A double sangha: celibate monastics and lay tantric householders (sngags pa, the 'white-robed, long-haired' community).
summary: The oldest school of Tibetan Buddhism, tracing itself to the 8th-century imperial translations and to Padmasambhava, Śāntarakṣita, Vimalamitra and the translator Vairocana. It arranges the whole Dharma as nine vehicles, keeps its own canon of Old Tantras (the Nyingma Gyubum), transmits teachings both by unbroken spoken lineage (kama) and by revealed treasures (terma), and holds the Great Perfection (Dzogchen, Atiyoga) as the summit of the path, systematized by Longchenpa and Jigme Lingpa.

name: Dzogchen (the Great Perfection, Atiyoga)

tradition.text: taught by Samantabhadra beyond time; first taught among humans by Garab Dorje in Oḍḍiyāna, then by Mañjuśrīmitra, Śrī Siṃha and Jñānasūtra; brought to Tibet by Vairocana, Vimalamitra and Padmasambhava in the 8th c.

scholarly.text: Great Perfection literature attested from the late 8th-10th c. (Dunhuang fragments incl. the Cuckoo of Awareness); the Seventeen Tantras and Nyingthig surface in the 11th-12th c.

transmissions_given.what: Nyingthig instruction adopted by Kagyu masters (e.g. the Third Karmapa Rangjung Dorje)

distinctive_positions: The ground (gzhi) is primordial purity (ka dag) and spontaneous presence (lhun grub); its three aspects are essence (ngo bo: empty), nature (rang bzhin: luminous) and compassion (thugs rje: all-pervading).
Awareness (rig pa) is distinguished from ordinary mind (sems): the path is recognizing awareness, not fabricating a meditative state.
Three series: mind (sems sde), space (klong sde) and instruction (man ngag sde); the Heart-essence (snying thig) belongs to the innermost secret cycle of the instruction series.
Cutting through (khregs chod) to primordial purity; direct crossing (thod rgal) of spontaneous presence through four visions; the fruit can include the rainbow body ('ja' lus).
Thoughts self-liberate (rang grol) in awareness; effort and contrivance are called a sickness (Kunjed Gyalpo).
Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa have one ground and two paths: recognition (Samantabhadra) and non-recognition (beings).
summary: The Great Perfection: the Nyingma (and Bön) teaching that the mind's nature, awareness (rig pa), is already perfect buddhahood — empty in essence, luminous in nature, all-pervading in responsiveness — and that liberation comes from recognizing it through a master's introduction and resting in it, rather than by constructing it. Transmitted through Garab Dorje, Mañjuśrīmitra, Śrī Siṃha, Jñānasūtra, Vimalamitra, Padmasambhava and Vairocana; organized in three series and systematized by Longchenpa.

name: Bön (Yungdrung Bön)
regions: Western Tibet (Zhang Zhung, Mount Kailash region)
exile communities (Dolanji, India; Triten Norbutse, Kathmandu)

tradition.text: taught by Tönpa Shenrab Miwoche in Ölmo Lungring (Tagzig) many millennia before Śākyamuni (a traditional Bön reckoning places his birth in 16,017 BCE); transmitted through Zhang Zhung to Tibet

scholarly.text: an organized Yungdrung Bön with its own canon is attested from the 11th c., when Shenchen Luga (996-1035) and others recovered treasure texts; earlier Tibetan and Zhang Zhung ritual traditions lie behind it

transmissions_given.what: shared Dzogchen and treasure frameworks; direction disputed (see dsp:bon-and-buddhism)

distinctive_positions: Bön is the teaching of Tönpa Shenrab Miwoche, a fully enlightened teacher from Ölmo Lungring in Tagzig, independent of and prior to Śākyamuni's Buddhism.
The teaching is ordered as nine ways (theg pa rim dgu), four causal ways and five fruitional ways, and in another scheme as four portals and a fifth, the treasury (sgo bzhi mdzod lnga).
Its Dzogchen (the A-khrid, the Dzogchen Yangtse Longchen and the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü) teaches the base of all (kun gzhi) inseparable from awareness (rig pa).
The swastika (g.yung drung) is the emblem of the indestructible and eternal; circumambulation is counter-clockwise.
Tibetan Buddhist historians' portrait of Bön as a pre-Buddhist or derivative religion is rejected by the Bön tradition.
notes: OPTIONAL per coverage map B6: 'Bön shares Dzogchen but lies outside the Buddhist family'. family set to 'shared' because Bön is neither Vedic nor an Indian śramaṇa tradition, yet shares Dzogchen, tantra and monasticism with the Buddhist family (decision by U45, logged in REPORT.md).
summary: The Bön religion of Tibet in its Yungdrung ('eternal', swastika) form: the teaching attributed to Tönpa Shenrab Miwoche, transmitted from Tagzig through Zhang Zhung, persecuted under the Tibetan kings, preserved in treasures recovered from the 10th-11th c., and organized monastically from Menri (1405). It has its own canon, nine ways, deities, monastic discipline and Great Perfection teachings closely parallel to the Nyingma, while insisting on its separate origin.

name: Longchen Nyingthig (the Heart-essence of the Great Expanse)

tradition.text: revealed as a mind treasure to Jigme Lingpa in visions of Longchenpa (from 1757)

distinctive_positions: The most widely practised Nyingma cycle: ngöndro, guru sādhana (Rigdzin Düpa), ḍākinī practice (Yumka) and Dzogchen instruction (Yeshe Lama) in one mind-treasure.
Received by Jigme Lingpa from Longchenpa in three visions; it condenses the Nyingthig Yabzhi.
summary: The mind-treasure cycle of Jigme Lingpa, received in visions of Longchenpa, which became the main Nyingma framework for preliminaries, guru yoga and Dzogchen, spread by Jigme Lingpa's disciples and Patrul Rinpoche.

name: Jangter (the Northern Treasures)

tradition.text: treasures revealed by Rigdzin Gödem in 1366 at Zangzang Lhadrak

distinctive_positions: Holds the Gongpa Zangthal ('Unobstructed Intention of Samantabhadra'), a Dzogchen treasure containing the Aspiration of Samantabhadra.
Seat: Dorje Drak monastery, one of the principal Nyingma monasteries.
summary: The tradition of the Northern Treasures revealed by Rigdzin Gödem (1337-1409), including the Dzogchen cycle Kuntuzangpo Gongpa Zangthal, later centred on Dorje Drak monastery.

name: Peling (the treasure tradition of Pema Lingpa)

tradition.text: treasures revealed by Pema Lingpa from 1476 (the Burning Lake, Mebar Tsho)

distinctive_positions: Bhutan's own Nyingma treasure tradition, with the Kunzang Gongdü cycle and sacred dances; carried by Pema Lingpa's three reincarnation lines (moderate confidence).
summary: The lineage of the Bhutanese treasure revealer Pema Lingpa (1450-1521), central to Nyingma practice and ritual culture in Bhutan.

name: Dudjom Tersar (the New Treasures of Dudjom)
distinctive_positions: Treasures of Dudjom Lingpa and of his reincarnation Dudjom Jigdral Yeshe Dorje, including Dzogchen instructions on 'buddhahood without meditation'.
summary: The recent treasure lineage of Dudjom Lingpa (1835-1904) and Dudjom Rinpoche Jigdral Yeshe Dorje (1904-1987), widely practised in exile communities.

name: Chokling Tersar (the New Treasures of Chokgyur Lingpa)
distinctive_positions: Treasures revealed by Chokgyur Lingpa, often jointly with Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and codified by Jamgön Kongtrul, notably the Tukdrub Barche Künsel guru sādhana.
summary: The recent treasure lineage of Chokgyur Dechen Lingpa (1829-1870), closely tied to the Rimé masters.

name: Zhang Zhung Nyengyü (the Oral Transmission of Zhang Zhung)
alt_names: the Aural Transmission of Zhang Zhung

tradition.text: an unbroken oral lineage never hidden as treasure; Tapihritsa taught Gyerpung Nangzher Löpo in the 8th c.

distinctive_positions: Bön Dzogchen held to have been transmitted orally without interruption (not a treasure); twenty-four masters of the lineage are said to have attained the rainbow body.
summary: The principal Dzogchen lineage of Bön, whose teaching passed from the Nine Buddhas of the mind transmission to Tapihritsa and Gyerpung Nangzher Löpo and was set down in four cycles (outer, inner, secret, innermost) plus the experiential transmission.

name: New Bön (Bön Sar)

scholarly.text: from c. the 14th c.; strengthened in the 18th-19th c.

distinctive_positions: Integrates figures and treasures shared with the Nyingma (Padmasambhava as a form of Drenpa Namkha's lineage) into Bön; regarded with reserve by Yungdrung Bön monastics (low confidence).
notes: Optional (Bön). Reconstructed from general knowledge; names of founders and texts omitted rather than guessed (see REPORT.md gaps).
summary: A current within Bön, attested from the late medieval period, that integrates treasures and figures shared with the Nyingma; distinguished from the 'Eternal' Yungdrung Bön.
